Earnings Call Transcript
Boeing (BA) Q3 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
By

Motley Fool Transcribing

–

Oct 29, 2025 at 12:58PM EST




Image source: The Motley Fool.


DATE
Wednesday, Oct. 29, 2025 at 10:30 a.m. ET
CALL PARTICIPANTS
President and Chief Executive Officer — Kelly Ortberg
Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer — Jay Malave
Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email
[email protected]
RISKS
777X Program Delay
— Management recorded a $4.9 billion non-cash charge in Q3 2025 due to delays in certification and first delivery of the 777-9, with first customer delivery of the 777-9 now expected in 2027 instead of 2026, resulting in higher costs for rework, production, and customer concessions.
2026 Cash Flow Headwinds
— Jay Malave stated, Cash usage for the 777X program is expected to be higher in 2026, representing a headwind relative to prior expectations of $2 billion. Cash usage for the 777X is expected to be higher in 2026 as the program builds inventory and experiences limited advances and delivery payments.
TAKEAWAYS
Revenue
-- $23.3 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2025, 30% increase in revenue compared to the prior year in the third quarter of 2025, primarily from higher commercial deliveries and defense volume.
Core Loss Per Share
-- $7.47 core loss per share in Q3 2025, including a $6.45 per share impact from the 777X program charge.
Free Cash Flow
-- Positive free cash flow of $238 million in Q3 2025, driven by higher commercial deliveries and improved working capital.
Commercial Airplane Deliveries
-- 160 units delivered in Q3 2025, the highest since 2018, including 121 737s and 24 787s delivered in the quarter; BCA revenue rose nearly 50% to $11.1 billion in Q3 2025.
BCA Operating Margin
-- Negative 48.3% operating margin for Boeing Commercial Airplanes in Q3 2025, impacted by the 777X charge.
Net Airplane Orders
-- 161 net orders in Q3 2025, highlighted by 57 787s for Turkish Airlines and 30 737-8s for Norwegian; backlog stands at $535 billion with over 5,900 airplanes.
737 Production Rate
-- Increased to 42 per month in October after stabilizing at 38; management confirmed further increments will occur in five-unit steps with at least six months between rate hikes, as stated on the earnings call.
FAA Delegation
-- The FAA granted Boeing limited delegation authority to issue airworthiness certificates for certain 737 MAX and 787 airplanes during the quarter.
777X Program Charge
-- $4.9 billion non-cash charge recorded in Q3 2025, driven by certification delays, higher expected costs, and rework.
Defense, Space & Security (BDS) Revenue
-- $6.9 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2025, a 25% increase compared to the prior year, on 30 aircraft and 2 satellite deliveries; operating margin improved to 1.7% in Q3 2025.
BDS Orders and Backlog
-- $9 billion in orders in Q3 2025 and a record $76 billion backlog in Q3 2025, including a $2.8 billion US Space Force SATCOM contract and $2.7 billion in PAC-3 seeker multi-year production contracts signed.
Global Services (BGS) Revenue
-- $5.4 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2025, up 10% compared to the prior year; operating margin at 17.5% in Q3 2025, with $8 billion in orders in Q3 2025 and a year-to-date book-to-bill ratio of 1.2 for the first nine months of 2025.
Cash and Liquidity
-- Ended Q3 2025 with $23 billion in cash and marketable securities and a debt balance of $53.4 billion as of Q3 2025; $10 billion in undrawn revolving credit facilities as of Q3 2025.
Capital Expenditures
-- Capital expenditures for calendar year 2025 are trending toward $3 billion; increased investment is planned in Charleston and St. Louis for future production rates and facility expansions.
M&A Activity
-- The company expects to close the Spirit AeroSystems acquisition and Jefferson digital business sale soon, with the Jefferson closing likely before Spirit.
SUMMARY
Boeing

(
BA

0.44%
)
reported a $4.9 billion non-cash charge in Q3 2025 and a new 777-9 delivery timeline of 2027, citing unanticipated certification process challenges under revised FAA requirements. Defense segment momentum continued, with backlog reaching a record $76 billion in Q3 2025 and key wins such as the $2.8 billion US Space Force SATCOM contract and multiple multi-year deals. BCA achieved its highest delivery volume since 2018 in Q3 2025, and BGS maintained double-digit margins and robust year-to-date order intake. The company generated positive free cash flow in Q3 2025 and increased the 737 production rate, with further incremental rate hikes dependent on system stability and supply chain readiness. Major facility expansions are underway in Charleston to support further 787 production rate ambitions, with capital allocation reflecting a focus on growth and operational resilience.
Kelly Ortberg confirmed, "we still expect the business to return to historical performance levels as we continue to drive execution and transition to new contracts with tighter underwriting standards."
Kelly Ortberg emphasized, "We're increasing production rates. We turned cash positive in the quarter, and we're winning in the market."
The BDS segment demonstrated operational improvements with minor cost updates on specific programs, while overall stability and profitability trends were highlighted in Q3 2025.
Management continues to prioritize disciplined rate transitions and rigorous adherence to performance metrics before further production increases.
FAA's newly granted limited delegation authority was characterized as a milestone, yet broader certification hurdles for the 777X remain unresolved, directly impacting program schedules and cost forecasts.
INDUSTRY GLOSSARY
Traveled Work
: Manufacturing tasks completed out of sequence or after a unit leaves its designated workstation, often resulting in increased rework and costs.
TIA (Type Inspection Authorization)
: FAA authorization allowing flight tests to count toward certification credit in the aircraft development process; delays in TIA can impede certification and delivery schedules.
Book-to-Bill Ratio
: The ratio of net new orders received to products delivered during a specified period, used to gauge demand and backlog growth.
BCA
: Boeing Commercial Airplanes segment, responsible for commercial jet manufacturing and services.
BDS
: Boeing Defense, Space & Security segment, focused on military, government, and space systems.
BGS
: Boeing Global Services segment, offering parts, logistics, maintenance, and digital solutions to commercial and defense customers.

Thanks, Kelly, and good morning, everyone. Let me start by saying that it has been an honor to join Boeing at such an important time in the company's history. Free cash flow was positive $238 million in the quarter, primarily reflecting higher commercial deliveries and working capital that improved compared to both the prior year and the prior quarter.
Importantly, this was the first positive free cash flow quarter since 2023 and serves as an important progress point in our company's recovery. These free cash flow results were better than expectations in July, driven by higher commercial deliveries, as well as the potential DOJ payment shifting to the fourth quarter. Turning to BCA on the next page. BCA delivered 160 airplanes in the quarter, the highest quarterly delivery total since 2018. Revenue was up nearly 50% to $11.1 billion, primarily reflecting higher deliveries compared to last year. Operating margin of negative 48.3% was impacted by the charge on the 777X program.
BCA booked 161 net orders in the quarter, including 57 787 airplanes for Turkish Airlines and 30 737-8 airplanes for the Norwegian group. Backlog in the quarter ended at $535 billion and includes more than 5,900 airplanes with the 737 and 787 both sold firm into the next decade. Now let's click down to the commercial programs. The 737 program delivered 121 airplanes in the quarter, including 41 in September. On production, the factory stabilized at 38 per month in the quarter. Importantly, we jointly agreed with the FAA in October to increase to 42 per month, and the program is now focused on continuing to drive a stable production system as they transition to this new rate.
Spirit continues to deliver fuselages with improved quality and flow, which sets us up well for both our future production ramp and the planned reintegration. That transaction is still expected to close this year. The quarter ended with approximately five 737-8s built prior to 2023, down 15 from the second quarter. Importantly, we completed the rework on the last of these airplanes and shut down the shadow factory in the third quarter. On the 787, we delivered 24 airplanes in the third quarter and ended with approximately ten 787 airplanes in inventory that were built prior to 2023, down five from last quarter. We still expect to deliver these airplanes through 2026, which is aligned with our customers' fleet planning requirements. Finally, on 777X, during the quarter, we recorded a $4.9 billion loss provision net of a cost base extension benefit to reset development and production schedule on the program, with first delivery now expected in 2027 versus the prior expectation of 2026.
To provide more background and color, we received approval to begin the second phase of certification flight test in early 2025 and had anticipated authorization to start the next major phase of certification flight testing in the third quarter. Given this delay and our assessment of the timeline to enter future certification phases, we have shifted our flight test and production schedules to reflect these learnings. We now expect the next major phase to start later this year or early 2026.
The certification program delay coupled with our reassessment of production cost constitute the basis for the incremental loss provision this quarter. The charge amount includes additional customer concessions, the cost of incremental rework on built aircraft, learning curve adjustments, and the carrying cost of production operations spread out over a longer period of time. On a comparable basis to last year's total charges on the program, the costs are higher due to rework on built aircraft, incremental production disruption, and learning curve adjustments. Start the cash profile. We see two impacts. The first is related to delivery timing, where we expect headwinds of about $2 billion in 2026 as deliveries move to the right.
This converts to a tailwind later in the decade as we deliver delayed units. Second, the cash roll-off of the $4.9 billion accounting charge is expected to be spread into the next decade. While disappointing, the reset allows us to operate to a higher confidence plan and allows our customers to manage their operations accordingly. As Kelly mentioned, this confidence also stems from our completion of dry run flight tests.
